title: Alphabetic Index and Tabular List

sections.learningObjectives:
- Locate main terms, subterms, and cross-references in the ICD-10-CM Alphabetic Index.
- Identify the correct Tabular List chapter, category, subcategory, and code for a given documented diagnosis.
- Apply coding conventions and instructional notes (Includes, Excludes1, Excludes2, Code first, Use additional code) to select and sequence codes.
- Distinguish index features such as nonessential and essential modifiers, eponyms, and the Tables of Neoplasms, Drugs and Chemicals, and External Causes.
- Recognize the medical office assistant's role and limits in diagnosis coding, including escalating unclear or unsupported diagnoses.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Think of the Alphabetic Index like the index at the back of a big book: it points you to the right page (or code) before you look at the details.

### Question 2

Finding a word in the index is only half the job; you still open the actual page to make sure it is the right, complete answer.

### Question 3

The index has four helpful 'helper lists': one for diseases and injuries, one for tumors, one for medicines, and one for how injuries happened.

### Question 4

Words in parentheses are like optional extra hints in a recipe; the dish is the same whether or not you read them.

### Question 5

An indented subterm is like a smaller, more specific folder tucked inside a big folder; it changes which file you actually pick.

### Question 6

'See' is like a traffic sign that says you must turn onto another road to reach your destination.

### Question 7

'See also' is like a librarian saying, 'You might also like this other shelf,' but you do not have to go there.

### Question 8

A disease named after a person can be found under that person's name and under the word 'disease,' like having two doors into the same room.

### Question 9

A default code is like the plain-vanilla option you pick when you do not yet know the flavor.

### Question 10

The index is organized A to Z, like a phone book, so you can flip straight to the word you need.

### Question 11

You look up the thing that happened ('fracture') first, and the place it happened (the femur) is a smaller note underneath it.

### Question 12

The tumor table is like a big grid: pick the body part down the side and the kind of tumor (harmless vs. harmful) across the top.

### Question 13

Poisoning is like taking too much of a medicine by mistake or on purpose; an adverse effect is when the right amount still makes you feel bad.

### Question 14

External cause codes are like answering 'how did it happen?' after you know 'what got hurt.'

### Question 15

The Tabular List is split into 21 big sections called chapters, each covering a family of conditions.

### Question 16

The chapters are like shelves in a library grouped by subject (heart, lungs, etc.), not sorted A to Z.

### Question 17

A three-character code is like a chapter-level label: it names the general topic but not the fine details yet.

### Question 18

Every diagnosis code starts with a letter and can grow up to seven characters long as more detail is added.

### Question 19

A, D, and S are like telling whether it is the first visit, a follow-up visit, or a later problem left over from the original injury.

### Question 20

If the problem is only on the left, you pick the 'left' box, just like choosing left vs. right shoes.

### Question 21

'Includes' is like a label on a storage bin that names some of the items you might find inside it.

### Question 22

Excludes1 is like two puzzle pieces that cannot be in the same picture; you can use one or the other, not both.

### Question 23

Excludes2 is like saying, 'That item lives on a different shelf, but you can take from both shelves if you need both.'

### Question 24

'Code first' is like saying the cause gets listed at the top of the page, and the effect follows below it.

### Question 25

'Use additional code' is like a reminder to also write down the related condition, so the whole picture is captured.

### Question 26

A manifestation is like a symptom that shows up because of a bigger cause; you list the cause first, then the symptom it produced.

### Question 27

A combination code is like a two-in-one label that describes both a condition and something that goes along with it.

### Question 28

NOS is when the chart just is not specific enough; NEC is when the chart is specific but there is no exact code for it yet.

### Question 29

Z codes are like labels for 'why the person came in,' such as a checkup or a family history, even when they are not sick.

### Question 30

External cause codes are like the 'what happened' note that goes next to the 'what got hurt' code.

### Question 31

The principal diagnosis is like the headline of a news story: it is the main reason the person came to the hospital.

### Question 32

If the doctor only knows the symptom so far, you write down the symptom; you do not make up a bigger answer.

### Question 33

'Rule out' means the doctor is still checking, so you write down the symptoms you do know, not the guess you do not know yet.

### Question 34

The diabetes is the main cause, so it goes first, and the eye problem it caused goes right after it.

### Question 35

You look up the name of the sickness ('pneumonia'), not the place it lives ('lung').

### Question 36

When several small labels are under one big heading, you pick the one that best describes what the doctor actually wrote.

### Question 37

'Acute' and 'chronic' are like the difference between a sudden storm and a long season; they are different weather, so they get different labels.

### Question 38

If one label already says everything, you use that one label instead of two smaller ones.

### Question 39

If both arms are in casts, you use the 'both' label, not two separate 'one arm' labels.

### Question 40

A sequela is like the scar left after a cut heals; you describe the scar now, then note it came from the old cut.

### Question 41

To tell the whole story of a poisoning, you note what the person took, whether it was on purpose or by accident, and what harm it caused.

### Question 42

If a medicine taken the right way causes a problem, you name the problem first and then say which medicine caused it.

### Question 43

Underdosing is like only taking half of the medicine the doctor said to take, whether on purpose or by accident.

### Question 44

Be as specific as the doctor's note allows, but never more specific than the note actually says.

### Question 45

Only some codes have a special last box that needs filling in; the code itself tells you when it does.

### Question 46

Every empty slot gets its own spacer block so the last character lands exactly where it belongs.

### Question 47

The code is like the price tag's description: if it is wrong, the store (the payer) may not pay for the right thing.

### Question 48

When a note is fuzzy, the safe move is to ask the doctor what they meant instead of making up an answer.

### Question 49

Upcoding is like writing a bigger price on a small item; it is dishonest and can get the practice in trouble.

### Question 50

When a puzzle is too hard, you ask a teacher for help instead of scribbling any answer.

### Question 51

The notes are like the fine print rules on a game board; skip them and you will make the wrong move.

### Question 52

The index is the map that gets you close, and the Tabular List is the sign at the door that confirms you are in the right room.

### Question 53

Brackets are like a translator's note, giving you another way to say the same medical word.

### Question 54

The colon is like the dot before a list: it says 'here come the items that belong to this note.'

### Question 55

'With' is like a plus sign connecting two related things, so they are coded as a pair.

### Question 56

NEC is for a very specific thing that just does not have its own exact code yet, so it goes in the closest matching box.

### Question 57

NOS is like answering 'the blue one' when you know the color but not the exact style; it is honest about what is not known.

### Question 58

If the note does not say which side, you ask the doctor instead of guessing left or right.

### Question 59

Pregnancy-related codes live in their own special 'O' chapter, like a dedicated shelf for baby-related care.

### Question 60

When the pregnancy issue is the main reason for the visit, the pregnancy code goes first, ahead of other chapters.

### Question 61

Besides 'how it happened,' you can also note 'where it happened' and 'what the person was doing.'

### Question 62

The assistant is like a careful helper who copies the doctor's labeled answer onto the right form and asks when unsure.

### Question 63

You look up the name of the ear problem ('otitis') and then narrow it down to the middle part ('media').

### Question 64

It is like zooming in: whole library (chapter), then shelf (category), then section (subcategory), then the one book (code).

### Question 65

After the first three characters name the topic, the next characters add fine details like where and how bad it is.

### Question 66

Every diagnosis code begins with a letter, like how every sentence begins with a capital letter.

### Question 67

The index is a starting map; you still check the real page to make sure the code is complete and has no special rules.

### Question 68

'Essential' here does not mean 'important'; it means the high blood pressure has no single known cause, so it is called primary.

### Question 69

When high blood pressure and heart trouble are connected, they share one combined label instead of two separate ones.

### Question 70

Diabetes is a big heading; when it causes trouble in the eyes or kidneys, you add a note for each trouble spot.

### Question 71

A screening is a 'just checking' visit, so it gets a 'checkup' label, not a 'sickness' label.

### Question 72

A 'history of' code is like a note that something happened before but is not happening now.

### Question 73

The rules are like grammar for a shared language: they make sure everyone writes codes the same, correct way.

### Question 74

The code's 'last-box' meanings are written on the same page in the Tabular List where the code itself lives.

### Question 75

'A' marks the first round of real fixing of the break, like the very first trip to get it treated.

### Question 76

'S' is for the leftover problem that shows up long after the injury healed, like a stiff joint from an old break.

### Question 77

If your first word is not in the index, try a nearby word or follow the index's own 'look here' signs until you find it.

### Question 78

The Tabular List shows the left, right, or both options, so you confirm the side there.

### Question 79

ICD-10-CM is the big dictionary of 'what is wrong or why they came in,' not a list of surgeries or medicine doses.

### Question 80

The index gives you a short code that is often missing its last pieces; the Tabular List is where you fill in the rest.

### Question 81

If there is no one big label that covers everything, you use several smaller labels, one for each problem, in the right order.

### Question 82

If someone asks you to change the label to one that is not true, the right move is to say no and tell a supervisor.

### Question 83

Chapter titles are like the signs over library aisles, telling you which body system or topic lives down each aisle.
